🇳🇵 Nepal–Tibet Border Avalanche & Flood | 26 August 2026 A major ice–rock avalanche near the Nepal–Tibet border triggered a cascading hazard: a large glacier mass collapsed from high elevation, sending ice, rock and sediment into the Lhende Khola. A new catastrophe has hit Nepal mere weeks after a deadly flood which killed over a thousand people… this time claiming an entire mountain. Dramatic footage has emerged of the moment the mountainside collapsed along the Kali Gandaki River, with a large section breaking apart and sliding directly into the river. The incident comes just one month after the 26th August glacier-and-rock collapse in the Langatang region which triggered apocalyptic flooding, claiming the lives of more than 3,000 people and left thousands more missing. While happening in very close proximity to that disaster, this latest incident cannot automatically be described as having been caused by it. Scientists have, however, warned that warming temperatures, glacier retreat and thawing mountain permafrost are making the Himalayan slopes increasingly unstable.

A major landslide in Manang has raised the risk of a mud-filled flood in the Marsyangdi River, leaving locals worried and scared. According to the District Administration Office, the landslide has not completely blocked the Marsyangdi River. However, a large amount of mud has entered the river, increasing the risk of flooding in downstream areas. Assistant Chief District Officer Krishna Prasad Poudel has urged people living along the river and nearby areas to remain highly alert. Authorities have also advised people to avoid unnecessary movement near the riverbanks and stay in safe places. #nepalinlast24hours

Rescuers dig through deep snow at the base of Nepal’s Himlung Himal as the desperate search continues for 12 people still missing after a deadly avalanche. Four bodies have now been recovered after the avalanche slammed into the 23,379-foot mountain’s base camp on Sunday, according to the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association. Helicopters are ferrying rescue teams into the remote area as crews comb through the snow. The workers and guides were preparing the mountain for the autumn climbing season when disaster struck. Foreign climbing clients had not yet reached the mountain.
